question: What is the main job of pulmonary surfactant inside the tiny air sacs (alveoli)?

options.A: To stimulate the diaphragm to contract during inspiration
options.B: To warm incoming air before it reaches the bronchioles
options.C: To transport oxygen directly into the bloodstream
options.D: To lower surface tension and prevent alveolar collapse

explanation: You've got this! Surfactant acts like a special coating that reduces surface tension inside the tiny air sacs, keeping them open and stable so breathing is easy. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T9#GNS213_U2_T9_h1)

question: What happens inside your chest when your diaphragm contracts to take in a normal breath?

options.A: Surface tension increases to make the lung tissue stiffer
options.B: Intrapleural pressure decreases to draw air into the lungs
options.C: Intrapleural pressure increases to force air out of the lungs
options.D: The chest wall pushes inward to compress the lung tissue

explanation: Great thinking! When your diaphragm moves down and your chest expands, the pressure inside drops below the outside air pressure, naturally sucking air in. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T9#GNS213_U2_T9_h1)

question: What is the main physical problem for a patient with an obstructive lung disorder?

options.A: Inability of the chest wall to expand at all
options.B: Total absence of blood flow through the capillaries
options.C: Complete destruction of the pulmonary surfactant
options.D: Difficulty getting air out of the lungs quickly

explanation: Spot on! Obstructive diseases narrow or trap air inside the airways, making it really hard for patients to breathe air out fast. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T9#GNS213_U2_T9_h2)

question: How do restrictive lung disorders mainly affect how the lungs work?

options.A: They trap large volumes of stale air inside the alveoli
options.B: They increase airway resistance specifically during expiration
options.C: They decrease the total capacity and expansion of the lungs
options.D: They lower the heart rate to slow down blood circulation

explanation: You're doing great! Restrictive disorders make the lung tissue or chest wall stiff, so the lungs just cannot expand to hold a normal volume of air. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T9#GNS213_U2_T9_h2)

question: What causes a high ventilation-perfusion mismatch, like when someone has a pulmonary embolism?

options.A: Air reaches the alveoli, but blood flow is blocked
options.B: Deoxygenated blood bypasses the lungs entirely through a shunt
options.C: Blood flows normally, but the airways are completely filled with pus
options.D: Surface tension drops so low that the alveoli permanently swell

explanation: Well done! A pulmonary embolism blocks blood flow past the air sacs, meaning air gets in fine, but there's no blood there to pick it up. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T9#GNS213_U2_T9_h3)

question: Why does a pulmonary shunt cause very low blood oxygen that doesn't easily fix with standard oxygen therapy?

options.A: Excess carbon dioxide blocks the hemoglobin binding sites permanently
options.B: Surfactant production stops completely, causing widespread lung collapse
options.C: Blood bypasses unventilated alveoli, so it never gets oxygen to pick up
options.D: The heart pumps too slowly to push blood through the narrowed pulmonary veins

explanation: Exactly. If blood flows past collapsed or fluid-filled sacs without getting oxygen, adding extra oxygen to room air can't reach that blocked blood! [learn more](GNS213_U2_T9#GNS213_U2_T9_h3)

question: Which major structural change happens in the lungs of someone with emphysema?

options.A: Thickening of the pleural space with fibrous scar tissue
options.B: Destruction of alveolar walls and loss of lung elasticity
options.C: Permanent blockage of the main pulmonary artery by clots
options.D: Excessive production of watery fluid inside the pleural cavity

explanation: You got it! Emphysema breaks down the walls of the air sacs and destroys the elastic fibers, making it hard for the lungs to bounce back when breathing out. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T9#GNS213_U2_T9_h4)

question: Why do advanced emphysema patients often end up with a flattened diaphragm and hard-working breathing muscles?

options.A: Scar tissue in the pleural lining pulls the diaphragm upward into the neck
options.B: Loss of pulmonary blood flow weakens the intercostal muscle fibers
options.C: Thick mucus plugs block the trachea and force the chest wall to expand
options.D: Air trapping hyperinflates the lungs and pushes the diaphragm downward

explanation: Makes total sense! Trapped air keeps the chest inflated like a balloon, flattening the diaphragm and making it tired and less efficient. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T9#GNS213_U2_T9_h4)

question: What is the primary change in lung tissue for a patient with pulmonary fibrosis?

options.A: Accumulation of watery transudate in the pleural cavity
options.B: Dilation and destruction of the small alveolar air sacs
options.C: Hypersecretion of thick mucus in the large main bronchi
options.D: Replacement of normal lung tissue with stiff scar tissue

explanation: Brilliant! Pulmonary fibrosis is all about chronic inflammation turning healthy lung tissue into stiff, non-stretchy scar tissue. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T9#GNS213_U2_T9_h5)

question: Which of these is considered an extrinsic cause of a restrictive lung disease?
explanation: You're doing awesome. 'Extrinsic' means the problem is outside the lung tissue itself—like a curved spine (scoliosis) squeezing the chest wall. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T9#GNS213_U2_T9_h5)

question: What is cor pulmonale?

options.A: Infection of the heart valves resulting from severe pneumonia
options.B: Narrowing of the coronary arteries due to chronic low blood oxygen
options.C: Weakening of the left ventricle caused by systemic high blood pressure
options.D: Right heart failure caused by primary lung or pulmonary vascular disease

explanation: Spot on! Cor pulmonale happens when lung problems create high pressure in the pulmonary vessels, forcing the right side of the heart to struggle and eventually fail. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T9#GNS213_U2_T9_h6)

question: How does long-term high blood pressure in the lungs (pulmonary hypertension) directly change the heart?

options.A: It shrinks the left atrium because less blood returns from the lungs
options.B: It causes the heart valves to stretch and leak due to low blood pressure
options.C: It weakens the left ventricle by reducing blood flow through the aorta
options.D: It causes the right ventricle to thicken and enlarge from working too hard

explanation: You've got it! Just like lifting heavy weights makes a bicep grow, the right ventricle bulks up (hypertrophies) when it has to push against high lung pressures. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T9#GNS213_U2_T9_h6)

question: What main trigger causes the kidneys to release erythropoietin in patients with chronic lung disease?

options.A: High levels of red blood cells in circulation
options.B: Increased blood pressure in the right atrium

explanation: Brilliant! When the kidneys sense low oxygen (hypoxemia) over a long time, they release erythropoietin to tell the bone marrow to make more red blood cells. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T9#GNS213_U2_T9_h7)

question: Why does long-term low blood oxygen sometimes lead to secondary polycythemia?

options.A: The liver releases clotting factors to repair damaged alveolar walls
options.B: The bone marrow responds to inflammation by producing excess white blood cells
options.C: The body tries to carry more oxygen by making extra red blood cells
options.D: Dehydrated blood vessels concentrate the existing red blood cells rapidly

explanation: You're nailing this! Making extra red blood cells is the body's clever way of packing more oxygen-carriers into the blood when air supply is low. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T9#GNS213_U2_T9_h7)
